picks.title: Efficient fucoxanthin production by fed-batch photo-fermentation cultivation of genetically engineered heterotrophic-growth Phaeodactylum tricornutum.
picks.hook: Engineered Phaeodactylum yields high fucoxanthin in fed‑batch photo‑fermentation.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to boost the commercial production of fucoxanthin, a valuable pigment, by improving the growth performance of the marine diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum. The researchers used metabolic engineering to convert an obligate photoautotrophic strain into one that can also grow heterotrophically, and then cultivated it in a fed‑batch photo‑fermentation system, which supplies nutrients continuously over time.

The engineered diatom was grown in a controlled bioreactor where light and an organic carbon source were provided together, allowing the culture to maintain high cell density while still producing the pigment. By feeding nutrients in a stepwise manner (fed‑batch), the process aimed to overcome the low biomass yields typical of traditional photo‑autotrophic cultivation.

The study reported that this approach achieved efficient fucoxanthin production, indicating that the engineered strain could generate higher biomass and pigment yields than conventional methods. 

These findings suggest a promising route to lower the cost and increase the scalability of fucoxanthin production, which could benefit both the algae industry and consumers who use the pigment in foods and cosmetics.
picks.why: Higher‑yield, cheaper fucoxanthin from engineered algae could make this antioxidant more accessible for food and health products.

picks.title: Stage-dependent nutrient assimilation, protein accumulation and microbial instability during fed-batch cultivation of Chlorella mutant strain in Chinese Baijiu brewing wastewater.
picks.hook: Chlorella mutant thrives in Baijiu brewing waste, boosting protein but faces microbial instability.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to see how a mutant strain of the microalga Chlorella could turn Chinese Baijiu brewing wastewater into protein‑rich biomass, despite the waste’s tendency to cause unstable loading and microbial failure.

The researchers grew the heavy‑ion‑mutagenized Chlorella mutant SLJ‑Q1 in a fed‑batch reactor using real Baijiu brewing wastewater as the feed. Growth was monitored over the early phase of the culture (days 0–10).

During this early phase the mutant achieved a specific growth rate of 0.069 /d, indicating steady cell division under the challenging wastewater conditions.

These results suggest that tailored algal strains can more reliably convert nutrient‑rich industrial waste into valuable protein, offering a potential route to sustainable bioproducts.
picks.why: It shows a way to harvest protein from waste streams, linking algae cultivation to greener food and feed production.

picks.title: Paralytic shellfish toxin production in Alexandrium minutum (Dinophyceae): Insights from omics integration using toxigenic and nontoxigenic recombinant progeny.
picks.hook: Omics of Alexandrium minutum reveal toxin pathways in recombinant progeny.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to uncover how the harmful algae Alexandrium minutum makes paralytic shellfish toxins, by comparing toxin‑producing and non‑producing offspring. The researchers grew both toxic and nontoxic recombinant progeny of the dinoflagellate and applied integrated omics—combined analysis of genomes, transcriptomes and metabolites—to trace the biosynthetic pathway.

By mapping gene activity and metabolic products in the two groups, they identified which genes and enzymes are active only in the toxin‑producing lines, shedding light on the steps that differ from the well‑studied cyanobacterial pathway.

The work shows that the dinoflagellate pathway involves a distinct set of genes, confirming that some sxt genes known from cyanobacteria also operate in Alexandrium, but with unique regulation.

Understanding these differences is valuable for monitoring harmful algal blooms and could inform strategies to mitigate toxin contamination in seafood.
picks.why: It helps improve detection and control of toxin‑producing algae that threaten seafood safety.

picks.title: Microalgae-based biosensing technologies for environmental monitoring and emerging food safety applications: Opportunities and challenges.
picks.hook: Microalgae‑based sensors offer new tools for environmental monitoring and food safety.
picks.article:
A recent study set out to examine how microalgae can be turned into reliable biosensors for monitoring the environment and checking food safety. The researchers reviewed the ways algae respond to pollutants by changing their photosynthesis, respiration, enzyme activity or overall metabolism, which can be recorded as optical or electrochemical signals.

They highlighted the main technical hurdles that still need to be overcome, such as keeping the algal cells alive, ensuring the sensors respond only to the target substance, and integrating the biological components with electronic transducers.

The review concluded that while microalgae offer a natural, low‑cost platform for detecting a wide range of contaminants, progress is needed to make the devices robust enough for real‑world deployment.

Understanding and solving these challenges could bring algae‑based sensors closer to practical use in water quality monitoring and food safety testing.
picks.why: Algae biosensors could provide affordable, real‑time detection of pollutants and contaminants, supporting safer water and food supplies.
